title: A Validation-Driven Bilevel Optimization Method for Mesh-Free PDE Solvers and Its Error Analysis
authors: Yongcun Song, Shangzhi Zeng, Jin Zhang, Lvgang Zhang
abstract: Mesh-free partial differential equation (PDE) solvers construct discrete systems from residuals at sampled points. These solvers fit coefficients in a parameterized trial representation and select solver-design parameters governing the representation, training-residual weighting, and regularization. These parameters strongly affect solution accuracy, yet existing selection strategies are largely tailored to particular solver classes. To address this limitation, we formulate a unified validation-driven bilevel optimization framework applicable across different solver classes, in which the lower level fits coefficients using training collocation residuals, while the upper level selects solver-design parameters using held-out validation residuals. For nonlinear PDEs, however, solving the nonlinear lower-level problem to high accuracy is costly, while the adjoint system is typically ill-conditioned and indefinite. To address this issue, we propose an efficient implicit hypergradient method that approximates the lower-level response using finite, warm-started damped Gauss-Newton (GN) updates. For the adjoint solve, we use the damped GN matrix to compute an initial adjoint and to precondition a finite number of minimum residual iterations. To quantify the errors introduced by these approximations, we derive local hypergradient error bounds that separate the contributions of the finite lower-level solve, adjoint damping, and the final adjoint residual. Combining this analysis with validation sampling bounds and residual stability, we relate validation residuals to PDE solution accuracy and establish error bounds for the computed PDE solution. Numerical experiments on several nonlinear PDEs, including a high-dimensional problem, demonstrate the accuracy and efficiency of the proposed method across Kansa, random feature and extreme learning machine, and physics-informed neural network solvers.

infographic.key_insight: A unified bilevel framework tunes mesh-free PDE solver designs using held-out validation residuals, with error analysis linking optimization approximations to solution accuracy.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach offers a common tuning strategy for representation, residual weighting, and regularization across several mesh-free solver families.
method: Fit solution coefficients on training collocation residuals; optimize solver-design parameters on validation residuals.
Approximate lower-level solutions with finite, warm-started damped Gauss–Newton updates.
Use the damped Gauss–Newton matrix to initialize and precondition adjoint iterations, with bounds separating key hypergradient errors.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments on several nonlinear PDEs, including a high-dimensional problem, report accuracy and efficiency across Kansa, random-feature/extreme-learning-machine, and physics-informed neural network solvers.
infographic.watch_item: The hypergradient guarantees are local, so practical reliability requires attention to lower-level convergence, damping, adjoint residuals, and validation sampling.
infographic.paper_title: A Validation-Driven Bilevel Optimization Method for Mesh-Free PDE Solvers and Its Error Analysis

title: A Calculus Gradient: Child Poverty, Mathematics Preparation, and First-Year College Performance at a Hispanic-Serving University
authors: Juan B. Gutiérrez
abstract: The San Antonio metropolitan area has one of the highest poverty rates among large U.S. metropolitan areas. Within Bexar County, where the city is located, child poverty varies widely across school districts. We link entrants of the city's public research university, a broad-access Hispanic-Serving Institution, to their sending schools and districts, and examine their preparation scores and first-year outcomes. Across the nation's school districts, enrollment in widely taken core courses (Algebra II, Geometry, Biology) shows little relation to child poverty, while enrollment in Calculus and Advanced Placement mathematics and science is far lower where child poverty is higher, nationally and within Bexar County. Among linked entrants, mathematics preparation differs with the school and district. Entrants with stronger mathematics preparation earn higher first-year grades in nearly every subject. Most entrants who do not return after the first year had unsuccessful courses, and mathematics is the largest single source of those outcomes. Among students who change major, mathematics is one of the subjects with grades furthest below their own averages. Within the same course and term, larger mathematics sections go with more unsuccessful outcomes for entrants with lower mathematics preparation, which identifies a hypothesis for testing smaller sections. Recorded between Fall 2014 and Fall 2019, these outcomes offer a reference point for change after the pandemic, test-optional admissions, and generative artificial intelligence. The analysis is reproducible; adapting it elsewhere requires local definitions and linkage validation. All results are associations among the students of one institution; establishing causes would require a designed study.

infographic.key_insight: Higher district child poverty is associated with lower access to advanced mathematics, while stronger mathematics preparation is associated with better first-year college grades across nearly every subject.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The findings can inform mathematics support and course-design studies for engineering pathways, especially for students entering with weaker preparation.
method: Compare core and advanced course enrollment with district child poverty nationally and in Bexar County.
Link university entrants to sending schools and districts to examine preparation and first-year outcomes.
Compare mathematics section size and unsuccessful outcomes within the same course and term.
infographic.evidence_signal: Records from Fall 2014 through Fall 2019 at one broad-access Hispanic-Serving university identify mathematics as the largest single source of unsuccessful course outcomes among entrants who did not return after their first year.
infographic.watch_item: These are observational associations, not causal effects; smaller mathematics sections remain a hypothesis requiring a designed study.
infographic.paper_title: A Calculus Gradient: Child Poverty, Mathematics Preparation, and First-Year College Performance at a Hispanic-Serving University

title: AI-Assisted Auto-formalization for Trustworthy Scientific Computing: Case Studies and Lessons Learned
authors: Mohit Tekriwal, Het Mankad, Naifeng Zhang, Keita Teranishi, Sahil Bhola, Daisuke Uchida
abstract: Agentic AI tools have recently had success in mathematical reasoning. Both general purpose coding agents such as Claude Code and Codex, and specialized mathematics agents such as Aristotle, have been used for formalizing mathematical problems such as Fermat's last theorem, Erdős problems and several IMO level math problems. However, much of these efforts are concentrated in the pure mathematics domain, which benefits from relatively self-contained theorem statements, fixed mathematical representation and extensive support in existing formal libraries. Applied mathematics, on the other hand, presents additional challenges because the source may describe a computational procedure or modeling transformation rather than a declarative theorem. In this work, we present a systematic study of AI-assisted auto-formalization for scientific computing (SC), a domain in applied mathematics central to U.S. Department of Energy applications. Through case studies spanning hierarchical abstraction layers in SC software stack, we evaluate not only whether AI agents can complete numerical proofs, but also where and why they fail across the stack. Our primary contribution is a cross-layer taxonomy of failure modes and an analysis of the form of expert feedback required at each layer to recover mathematical soundness. From these observations, we derive a workflow for recurring proof patterns and practical guidance for using AI agents while preserving mathematical soundness. Our results characterize both the practical value and the current limitations of AI-assisted formalization for trustworthy scientific computing.

infographic.key_insight: Trustworthy AI-assisted formalization in scientific computing requires expert feedback tailored to failure modes across abstraction layers.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The study offers workflow guidance for using AI agents to formalize scientific computing mathematics while preserving mathematical soundness.
method: Study AI-assisted formalization across scientific computing abstraction layers.
Classify failure modes and the expert feedback needed to recover soundness.
Derive workflows for recurring proof patterns.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports cross-layer case studies evaluating proof completion and failure causes, but provides no quantitative success rates.
infographic.watch_item: Computational procedures and modeling transformations can be harder to formalize than self-contained theorems and require careful expert interpretation.
infographic.paper_title: AI-Assisted Auto-formalization for Trustworthy Scientific Computing: Case Studies and Lessons Learned

title: Beyond PINNs: Boundary-Enriched Holomorphic Networks for Laplace Problems
authors: Andrei Vlad Nicula, Kalp Shah, Robert-Stefan Sofroni, Mihnea Andrei Bârsan, Agneya Bhardwaj, Jan Jelínek
abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) solve partial differential equations by penalizing their residual, but this formulation can be difficult to optimize for solutions with singular behaviour. We focus specifically on the two-dimensional Laplace equation, whose strong analytical structure allows the governing equation to be enforced directly in the neural representation. We compare a hybrid harmonic-neural model with a holomorphic neural network whose output is harmonic by construction and therefore requires only boundary training. We further enrich the holomorphic model with singular functions chosen according to the interior angle and boundary conditions at each junction of boundary segments. On six singular benchmarks, the enriched model is the most accurate of the neural models we compare. On the four with a closed-form solution, however, that solution lies in the span of the enrichment terms, and a least-squares fit of these terms alone is exact to rounding error. On Motz's problem and the cracked beam, the neural core reduces the relative error of the recovered leading singular coefficient from about $10^{-2}$, for a least-squares fit with the same four terms, to about $10^{-6}$, and on four variants whose solution has a smooth part outside the span, the network is $4\times10^{4}$ to $2\times10^{7}$ times more accurate than a fit of its singular terms alone; classical least-squares fits with more singular terms, or with harmonic polynomials and rational poles, are more accurate still. Our results demonstrate how exploiting problem-specific analytical structure can provide an alternative to base and residual PINNs for challenging scientific computing problems.

infographic.key_insight: For 2D Laplace problems, holomorphic networks enforce harmonicity by construction, while boundary-specific singular enrichment improves accuracy without PDE-residual training.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Encoding known analytical structure offers an alternative to residual-based PINNs for potential-field simulations with corner or boundary-junction singularities.
method: Use a holomorphic neural representation whose output is harmonic by construction.
Add singular functions selected from local interior angles and boundary conditions.
Train on boundary data and compare against neural and classical least-squares baselines.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across six singular benchmarks, the enriched model led the tested neural models; on Motz’s problem and the cracked beam, it reduced leading singular-coefficient relative error from about 10⁻² to 10⁻⁶ versus a four-term least-squares fit.
infographic.watch_item: Benefits depend on problem-specific enrichment: singular terms alone solve four closed-form benchmarks to rounding error, and richer classical fits can outperform the network.
infographic.paper_title: Beyond PINNs: Boundary-Enriched Holomorphic Networks for Laplace Problems

title: Nearly Minimax-Optimal Sample Complexity of Natural Policy Gradient with a Matching Information-Theoretic Lower Bound
authors: Asha Barua, Sajad Khodadadian
abstract: A fundamental question in reinforcement learning is how many sampled transitions are needed to learn a near-optimal policy, and whether direct policy optimization can attain this statistical limit. To answer this question, we consider natural policy gradient (NPG), a widely used policy optimization method. We study tabular finite-horizon Markov decision processes (MDPs) with known rewards and unknown horizon-dependent transition kernels, accessed through a generative model. Our sample-based NPG algorithms update the policy by backward sweeps and do not estimate transition probabilities. Under three different batch-size and step size schedules, we establish last-iterate guarantees with sample complexity $\widetilde O(SAH^4/\varepsilon^2)$, where $S$, $A$, and $H$ denote the number of states, the number of actions, and the horizon length, respectively. In this setting, horizon-dependent transition kernels contribute a factor of $H$ to our transition-query bound. Our information-theoretic lower bound of $Ω(SAH^4/\varepsilon^2)$ shows that the resulting $H^4$ dependence is unavoidable in the worst case, even for agents that select their queries adaptively. To the best of our knowledge, these are the first last-iterate guarantees for NPG whose sample complexity matches an information-theoretic lower bound up to logarithmic factors. Consequently, our results demonstrate that direct policy-space optimization through NPG can achieve the fundamental statistical limits of reinforcement learning while guaranteeing the performance of the final policy. Furthermore, for known kernels, we prove that exact NPG with a constant step size $η=1/H$ requires $Ω(H^2/\varepsilon)$ iterations in the worst case, matching the known upper bound for that step size.

infographic.key_insight: Natural policy gradient achieves near-minimax-optimal transition-query complexity of Õ(SAH⁴/ε²), with a matching Ω(SAH⁴/ε²) lower bound and guarantees for the final policy.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Direct policy optimization can reach fundamental sampling limits in tabular finite-horizon reinforcement learning without explicitly estimating transition probabilities.
method: Study known-reward MDPs with unknown, horizon-dependent transitions accessed through a generative model.
Update policies through backward-sweep natural policy gradient under three batch-size and step-size schedules.
Prove last-iterate upper bounds and an information-theoretic lower bound covering adaptive queries.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical guarantees rather than empirical benchmarks, including an Ω(H²/ε) worst-case iteration lower bound for exact NPG with known kernels and step size 1/H.
infographic.watch_item: The guarantees assume tabular MDPs, known rewards, and generative-model access; they do not establish equivalent performance with function approximation or online-only interaction.
infographic.paper_title: Nearly Minimax-Optimal Sample Complexity of Natural Policy Gradient with a Matching Information-Theoretic Lower Bound

title: Congestion-Aware Adaptive Routing for LLM Classification
authors: Yuan Guo, Stefanus Jasin, Chen-An Lin
abstract: Organizations use large language models (LLMs) to classify jobs that differ in uncertainty and the cost of errors. Querying additional models may improve accuracy, but it also incurs fees and increases congestion at shared servers. We study congestion-aware adaptive routing (CAAR) policies that adapt model selection and stopping decisions to observed outputs while accounting for the steady-state congestion they generate. The objective is to minimize the long-run average cost of misclassification penalties, query fees, and holding costs. We can represent CAAR policies as a mixture of decision trees, and derive exact holding costs for first-come-first-served servers with exponential service times and processor-sharing servers with general service times. We formulate a convex optimization problem with unique optimal model loads. Congestion prices capture the marginal system-wide holding costs of additional queries and guide routing and stopping decisions through a Bayesian dynamic program. We characterize optimal stopping decisions and identify models whose information does not justify their cost. A column-generation algorithm computes optimal CAAR policies and provides an explicit optimality-gap bound. We also bound the additional cost of limiting cascade depth relative to full-depth CAAR. Finally, under a common query-depth limit, cascades with a predetermined model order can be arbitrarily more costly than optimal CAAR, even when the order is randomized and stopping decisions adapt to observed outputs. Numerical experiments distinguish the benefits of adaptive model selection and congestion-aware design.

infographic.key_insight: Adapting both model choice and stopping to observed outputs and congestion minimizes long-run classification costs, while fixed-order cascades can be arbitrarily more costly under the same query-depth limit.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Shared LLM classification services can balance error penalties, query fees, and latency costs by pricing the congestion each additional query creates.
method: Represent adaptive routing policies as mixtures of decision trees and formulate a convex optimization problem.
Use marginal congestion prices in a Bayesian dynamic program to choose models and stopping decisions.
Compute policies with column generation and an explicit optimality-gap bound.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports numerical experiments separating the benefits of adaptive model selection and congestion-aware design, but provides no datasets or quantitative results.
infographic.watch_item: Exact holding-cost results rely on specified queueing assumptions: exponential service times for first-come-first-served servers or general service times under processor sharing.
infographic.paper_title: Congestion-Aware Adaptive Routing for LLM Classification

title: Expressive Shallow Networks for Physics-Informed Learning: Why Curvature-Aware Optimization and FP64 Are Not Enough
authors: Zachary Morrow, Yucheng Fu, Pratanu Roy, Michael Penwarden
abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) often struggle with high-frequency and high-order partial differential equations (PDEs) due to optimization stiffness and spectral bias, despite possessing sufficient approximation capacity. Existing remedies, including modified feature representations, domain decomposition, higher floating-point precision, and curvature-aware optimizers, can improve convergence but largely act as workarounds for optimization difficulties arising from deep architectures rather than addressing their underlying source. We investigate Physics-Informed Shallow Universal Polynomial Networks (PI-SUPNs), which replace deep nonlinear compositions with learnable polynomial expansions, retaining high approximation capacity within a shallow computational graph. On a high-frequency Helmholtz benchmark, PI-SUPNs are the only architecture to successfully recover the solution, while all competing models fail even under FP64 precision and curvature-aware optimization. However, experiments on higher vibrational modes of a fourth-order Euler-Bernoulli beam reveal that architectural improvements alone are insufficient: accurate solutions require the combination of PI-SUPNs, FP64 precision, and curvature-aware optimization. Additionally, Allen-Cahn experiments show that PI-SUPNs achieve lower solution and derivative errors at reduced computational cost, with more favorable loss landscapes than competing architectures. We also establish quasi-local approximation properties and spline-based convergence bounds for SUPNs. Our results show that shallow network architectures are an important mechanism for improving physics-informed trainability, but accurate solutions to the most challenging PDEs can still require FP64 precision and curvature-aware optimization.

infographic.key_insight: Shallow polynomial networks improve physics-informed trainability, but the hardest PDE benchmarks still require FP64 precision and curvature-aware optimization.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For high-frequency or high-order PDE solvers, changing network architecture can matter more than upgrading numerical precision or optimization alone.
method: Replace deep nonlinear compositions with learnable polynomial expansions in PI-SUPNs.
Evaluate architecture, precision, and curvature-aware optimization across PDE benchmarks.
Establish quasi-local approximation properties and spline-based convergence bounds.
infographic.evidence_signal: PI-SUPNs alone recovered the high-frequency Helmholtz solution among tested architectures; higher beam modes required PI-SUPNs plus FP64 and curvature-aware optimization, while Allen–Cahn tests showed lower solution and derivative errors at reduced computational cost.
infographic.watch_item: Benchmark successes do not establish universal superiority, and challenging cases retain the computational requirements of FP64 and curvature-aware optimization.
infographic.paper_title: Expressive Shallow Networks for Physics-Informed Learning: Why Curvature-Aware Optimization and FP64 Are Not Enough

title: Agentic Discovery of Simple Symbolic Inventory Policies
authors: Xi Chen, Yuze Chen, Baichuan Mo, Jie Ying, Yuan Zhou
abstract: Designing simple inventory policies becomes increasingly difficult as operational features and system configurations expand. We develop an Agentic Inventory-Policy Discovery System based on explicitly defined simple operational formula (SOF) policy and template classes. Large language models (LLMs) revise symbolic structures, while a numerical engine fits parameters separately for each instance and evaluates the induced policies. Multicriteria parent selection, state-specific operational diagnostics, and reusable symbolic motifs guide structural evolution. A three-stage progression develops shared templates across instances and configurations with varying state dimensions. Experiments on 15,600 instances spanning 50 demand distributions cover lead times, perishability, their combination, and lead times with limited customer patience. The discovered templates improve aggregate empirical performance over evaluated SOF benchmarks and are competitive with policies requiring more elaborate online computations. For a lost-sales system with a three-period lead time, we develop an average-cost decomposition and prove that, under specified demand and cost conditions, a capped dual-shortfall specialization of a discovered policy strictly outperforms every policy in the considered capped base-stock benchmark class. This analysis links the performance advantage to the discovered replenishment mechanism. Together, these results highlight the potential of agentic discovery to generate simple inventory policies with strong empirical performance and identify operational mechanisms amenable to rigorous theoretical analysis.

infographic.key_insight: LLM-guided symbolic search discovers simple inventory-policy templates that improve empirical performance and expose replenishment mechanisms suitable for mathematical analysis.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach offers compact decision rules for inventory systems with lead times, perishability, or limited customer patience, while fitting parameters separately for each instance.
method: LLMs revise symbolic policy structures; a numerical engine fits parameters and evaluates policies.
Multicriteria selection, state-specific diagnostics, and reusable symbolic motifs guide structural evolution.
A three-stage progression develops shared templates across instances and configurations with varying state dimensions.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation covers 15,600 instances across 50 demand distributions; discovered templates outperform evaluated simple-formula benchmarks in aggregate and are competitive with policies requiring more elaborate online computation.
infographic.watch_item: The strict theoretical advantage applies only to a specialized three-period lead-time setting under specified demand and cost conditions, not to every discovered template or configuration.
infographic.paper_title: Agentic Discovery of Simple Symbolic Inventory Policies

title: Finite-difference neural policy iteration for high-dimensional degenerate Hamilton--Jacobi equations
authors: Hee Jun Yang, Yeoneung Kim
abstract: We develop a finite-difference neural policy iteration method for high-dimensional degenerate Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman and Isaacs equations. Artificial viscosity yields a monotone finite-difference operator, and neural networks approximate the linear equations of semi-discrete policy iteration using local stencil values. This avoids global tensor-grid storage. For measurable feedbacks, we bound the propagation of evaluation, terminal, gradient, and control optimization errors by a geometrically weighted sum. Discrete comparison, consistency, and vanishing viscosity relate the approximation to the original degenerate equation. On coupled manufactured problems with rank-deficient diffusion, the method achieves lower mean errors than direct physics-informed neural networks at every tested dimension from five to fifty under equal training time. At fifty dimensions and $900$ seconds, the mean relative $L^2$ error over three paired seeds is about $40\%$ lower. Two-dimensional refinement attains $0.297\%$ error against the original degenerate solution, with independent grid references separating approximation error from viscosity bias. In a twenty-dimensional game with finite control sets, reusing policies reduces the measured time to a relative error of $5\%$ by $24.3\%$ compared with direct minimization of the same discrete residual with fresh samples at every update.

infographic.key_insight: Neural policy iteration with monotone finite differences tackles high-dimensional degenerate Hamilton–Jacobi equations without storing a global tensor grid.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach offers a memory-efficient route to high-dimensional optimal-control and differential-game PDEs with rank-deficient diffusion.
method: Add artificial viscosity to obtain a monotone finite-difference operator.
Use neural networks and local stencil values to approximate linear policy-evaluation equations.
Bound propagated evaluation and optimization errors, and connect the scheme to the original equation through vanishing viscosity.
infographic.evidence_signal: On manufactured problems, mean errors beat direct PINNs at every tested dimension from 5 to 50 under equal training time; at 50 dimensions and 900 seconds, mean relative L2 error was about 40% lower across three paired seeds.
infographic.watch_item: Artificial viscosity introduces bias, so accuracy against the original degenerate equation requires refinement and independent validation.
infographic.paper_title: Finite-difference neural policy iteration for high-dimensional degenerate Hamilton--Jacobi equations

title: A statistical measure of trust in generative AI
authors: Alina Ermilova, Valeria Yakupova, Nikita Sushko, Andrey Lovyagin, George Ovchinnikov, Maksim G. Sharaev
abstract: Trustworthiness is a crucial issue for generative AI, as modern models can produce convincing and confident responses even when their outputs are incomplete, unsupported, or wrong. The frequent absence of ground-truth knowledge or labels complicates verification of generative AI outputs. To address this issue, we propose a trustworthiness framework grounded in model-internal confidence calibrated against an external expert reference. We estimate per-token trustworthiness of a student generative model as the statistical typicality of each generated token relative to an expert model's distribution, where the expert is used as a distributional reference rather than as a source of factual verification labels. To this end, we introduce an AI ontology calibrator that leverages the student model's internal latent features and token-level output statistics to compute expert-reference acceptance scores. Combined with traditional token-level confidence, entropy, and perplexity statistics, calibrator scores yield a compact set of $15$ response-level indicators for correctness classification. Evaluated across BF program generation, mathematical problem solving, and medical question answering, combined calibrator and traditional indicators provide complementary reliability signal which could be used to build detectors of untrustworthy outputs and hallucinations. Remarkably, our experiments show that these detectors are transferable across domains, although transferability is not always symmetric.

infographic.key_insight: Token-level typicality relative to an expert model adds reliability signals beyond a generative model’s own confidence.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Combining expert-reference scores with standard confidence statistics could support detectors that flag potentially incorrect outputs across application domains.
method: Use an expert model’s token distribution as a reference, not as factual ground truth.
Train an AI ontology calibrator using student-model latent features and token-level output statistics to estimate expert-reference acceptance scores.
Aggregate calibrator scores with confidence, entropy, and perplexity into 15 response-level indicators for correctness classification.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluations on BF program generation, mathematical problem solving, and medical question answering show complementary reliability signals and cross-domain detector transfer, though transfer is not always symmetric.
infographic.watch_item: Agreement with an expert distribution does not establish factual correctness, and transfer performance may depend on the source and target domains.
infographic.paper_title: A statistical measure of trust in generative AI

title: Hierarchical randomized neural networks for efficiently and accurately finding multiple solutions of semilinear elliptic equations
authors: Jingying Hu, Jiao Li, Yufeng Xu, Jinyong Ying
abstract: Being able to find multiple solutions of a semilinear elliptic equation is a fundamental problem in scientific computing. In this paper, fully taking the advantages of randomized neural networks, we propose a new efficient and accurate method for identifying potentially as many solutions as possible. The new method is constructed from three aspects--initialization, optimization, a technique for acceleration and improving accuracy, two of which are innovative developments. Firstly, based on the basis functions of a randomized network and the sampling points, a characteristic matrix is introduced so that its singular value decomposition can be used to determine weakly variant search directions, followed by a newly developed algorithm to generate effective initial candidates. Then the good deflated Gauss-Newton method [see {\em A. Riley, et al., SIAM Journal on Scientific Computing 47~(5) (2025) A2963-A2987}] using an exponential deflation operator is adapted as the optimization to search for all multiple solutions. Local error estimate of a particular solution under some proper condition is given in terms of the neurons in the hidden layer and the sampling points for this newly designed method. Furthermore, to accelerate the computation and improve the solution accuracy, a new multilevel method based on hierarchical networks is designed. Without using any {\em a priori} information, several numerical tests show together with the multilevel method, the new method can not only accurately find multiple solutions with relative errors reaching $10^{-16}$ only in less than one-tenth computational cost for the best case, but also preserve the inherent symmetries of multiple solutions.

infographic.key_insight: Hierarchical randomized neural networks combine SVD-guided initialization, deflated optimization, and multilevel refinement to efficiently find multiple solutions of semilinear elliptic equations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could help computational engineers explore multiple nonlinear PDE solutions without requiring prior knowledge of their structure.
method: Use a characteristic matrix and its SVD to identify weakly varying search directions and generate initial candidates.
Apply good deflated Gauss–Newton optimization with exponential deflation to seek distinct solutions.
Use hierarchical network levels to accelerate computation and improve accuracy.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical tests report relative errors reaching 10⁻¹⁶, computational cost below one-tenth of the comparison cost in the best case, and preservation of solution symmetries.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish exhaustive solution discovery; accuracy and cost gains may depend on the problem, network size, and sampling.
infographic.paper_title: Hierarchical randomized neural networks for efficiently and accurately finding multiple solutions of semilinear elliptic equations

title: Symmetries, conservation laws, series solutions and singularity formation for the spherically symmetric Euler-Poisson equations in mass coordinates
authors: Adnan Shamaoon
abstract: Written in Lagrangian mass coordinates, the spherically symmetric Euler-Poisson equations for a polytropic gas become a single second-order equation for the radius $r(t,m)$ of the shell enclosing mass $m$, with adiabatic index $γ>1$ and entropy profile $S(m)$. We determine all point symmetries of this equation. Apart from time translation there is at most one scaling, except at the critical index $γ=4/3$, where a scaling exists for every entropy profile; these scalings are the entropy-fixed stabilisers of the two-parameter scaling group of the non-isentropic system, and we give the exact symmetry defect when $γ\neq4/3$. Noether's theorem singles out the profiles $S=Km^{14-10γ}$, for which a scaling is variational and gives a conservation law beyond energy; otherwise the scalings yield virial identities. We construct exact collapse solutions and reduce the self-similar problem to one ordinary differential equation. Using the Briot-Bouquet theorem we prove that the regular centre of self-similar and homologous collapse carries a convergent analytic expansion with free central amplitude, and we derive a Puiseux expansion at the stellar surface whose exponent is the polytropic index $1/(γ-1)$. In mass coordinates a density singularity is a zero of $r_m$ or of $r$; for the first kind we prove a Hopf-type fold law and an exact shell-crossing criterion for free-falling dust. Finally, linear perturbations of the critical Einstein-de Sitter collapse separate exactly into spherical Bessel profiles, with exponents solving $3κ^2+κ-2+μ=0$. All identities were checked by computer algebra, and the numerical statements rest on convergence studies of a second-order Lagrangian scheme, including a collapse with a free surface.

infographic.key_insight: Spherical Euler–Poisson dynamics in mass coordinates admit a unified analysis of symmetries, conservation laws, collapse expansions and density singularities, with special scaling structure at γ = 4/3.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The results provide analytical benchmarks for computational models of self-gravitating gas collapse and numerical detection of shell crossing.
method: Reduce the equations to one radius equation and classify point symmetries and Noether conservation laws.
Construct exact collapse solutions and prove convergent central expansions using the Briot–Bouquet theorem.
Derive surface expansions, singularity criteria and separated linear perturbation modes.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports computer-algebra checks of all identities and convergence studies of a second-order Lagrangian scheme, including collapse with a free surface.
infographic.watch_item: The analysis assumes spherical symmetry and a polytropic gas; extensions to multidimensional flows or more general equations of state are not established here.
infographic.paper_title: Symmetries, conservation laws, series solutions and singularity formation for the spherically symmetric Euler-Poisson equations in mass coordinates

title: Verifiable On-Policy Distillation
authors: Juntong Shi, Stefano Ermon, Jure Leskovec, Minkai Xu
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become a powerful approach for improving language-model reasoning, but its supervision is inherently sparse: a sequence-level verifier reward is propagated only through sampled trajectories and provides no direct signal for alternative actions. On-policy distillation (OPD) offers a complementary form of supervision by providing dense teacher feedback over the full next-token distribution, but this signal is not grounded in verified task outcomes. Simply co-optimizing the two objectives does not couple these signals: verifier feedback remains sparse and does not inform the dense teacher supervision. We introduce Verifiable On-Policy Distillation (VOPD), which transfers sparse verifier feedback into dense, verifier-grounded supervision. Our key observation is that the implicit-reward view of OPD places teacher supervision and verifier feedback in a common reward space while retaining a reward signal available for every next-token action. Under this view, VOPD projects verifier preference onto the teacher's implicit-reward direction and Rao--Blackwellizes the resulting signal over the full vocabulary, propagating verifier-grounded supervision to actions that were never sampled. The resulting objective can also be interpreted as adaptively extrapolating the distillation target according to teacher--verifier agreement. Across two teacher--student configurations and eight mathematical reasoning benchmarks, VOPD consistently improves both final performance and learning efficiency over vanilla OPD and other on-policy distillation baselines. Our code is available at https://github.com/juntongshi48/VOPD.

infographic.key_insight: VOPD turns sparse verifier feedback into dense, verifier-grounded next-token supervision, coupling outcome verification with teacher guidance.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For mathematical-reasoning model training, VOPD offers a way to improve performance and learning efficiency beyond standard on-policy distillation.
method: Express teacher supervision and verifier feedback in a shared implicit-reward space.
Project verifier preference onto the teacher’s implicit-reward direction.
Rao–Blackwellize over the full vocabulary to supervise even unsampled next-token actions.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across two teacher–student configurations and eight mathematical reasoning benchmarks, the abstract reports consistent gains in final performance and learning efficiency over vanilla OPD and other on-policy distillation baselines.
infographic.watch_item: Full-vocabulary teacher feedback may add computational overhead; the abstract does not quantify this cost.
infographic.paper_title: Verifiable On-Policy Distillation

title: Notes on Generative AI for Mathematical Research
authors: Shurui Liu
abstract: These notes describe how generative AI is now used to solve and to check research-level mathematics, with a focus on agents and their harnesses. For the proving agents Rethlas, Danus, and Pharos and the verification agent OSVerify, we explain the design principles, compare each with its base model, present case studies, and show how to use and contribute to them. We also briefly review the history of AI for mathematics and the community's reactions to it.

infographic.key_insight: Generative AI agents and their harnesses are being used to solve and check research-level mathematics.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The notes offer design principles and practical guidance for using and contributing to mathematical proving and verification agents.
method: Examine proving agents Rethlas, Danus, and Pharos and verification agent OSVerify.
Compare each agent with its base model and present case studies.
Explain agent design principles, usage, and contribution workflows.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports base-model comparisons and case studies but provides no quantitative results or evaluation details.
infographic.watch_item: Agent-generated proofs still require careful validation; the abstract does not establish verification guarantees.
infographic.paper_title: Notes on Generative AI for Mathematical Research

title: Late-Time Dynamics of Flow Matching: Distance Geometry and Learning
authors: Umberto Biccari, Junqing Huang, Kang Liu, Enrique Zuazua
abstract: Generative models transform simple random inputs into samples that resemble observed data. For a finite training set, a central question is how its geometry shapes the terminal dynamics and the probabilities assigned to individual samples. We address this question for flow matching with linear interpolation between independent Gaussian and empirical samples. The squared distance to the training set generates explicit paths contracting exponentially toward the nearest sample. We prove that exact trajectories restarted at prescribed late-time states approximate these paths uniformly over all elapsed times and compact sets of starting states away from Voronoi interfaces, with an error exponentially small in the inverse squared restart noise scale. The initial mass near interfaces controls the quadratic Wasserstein error between the exact and reference laws. For Gaussian and fixed Gaussian-tube restart laws, this gives a square-root rate in the restart noise scale, uniform over time, which a two-site example shows to be sharp in general. At ties, the Clarke subdifferential characterizes the graphical limit of the rescaled velocity field. This geometry motivates two learning methods: fitting the distance potential with value and gradient supervision, and fitting velocities along explicit contraction paths. A transport estimate separates initialization mismatch, velocity error, incomplete contraction, and endpoint allocation. MNIST experiments illustrate the distinct roles of support proximity, nearest-site retention, and feature fidelity. These results connect flow matching and score-based diffusion through a common limiting geometry and show how asymptotic analysis can inform the design and evaluation of generative models.

infographic.key_insight: At late times, flow matching toward finite training data follows nearest-sample contractions governed by distance geometry, with Voronoi interfaces controlling approximation error.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This geometry suggests tractable training targets and diagnostics that distinguish sample proximity, nearest-site retention, and feature fidelity.
method: Analyze exact trajectories against explicit exponentially contracting nearest-sample paths.
Fit the distance potential using value and gradient supervision, or fit velocities along contraction paths.
Separate transport error into initialization mismatch, velocity error, incomplete contraction, and endpoint allocation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The analysis establishes time-uniform square-root Wasserstein rates for Gaussian and fixed Gaussian-tube restarts, proves sharpness with a two-site example, and illustrates evaluation criteria on MNIST.
infographic.watch_item: Trajectory guarantees require late-time restarts away from Voronoi interfaces; mass near ties can limit distributional accuracy.
infographic.paper_title: Late-Time Dynamics of Flow Matching: Distance Geometry and Learning

title: Verifying the Outputs of PDE Solvers: From Finite Elements to Neural Surrogates
authors: Konstantinos Dovelos
abstract: Physics simulation outputs increasingly come from solvers that no expert inspects, such as third-party packages in automated pipelines, programs written by large language models (LLMs), and learned surrogates. In earlier work on cardiac pulsed field ablation, we proposed that solvers return a certificate with their answers. The certificate consists of an admissible potential and an exactly charge-conserving current, and a small independent checker turns it into guaranteed error bounds against a written specification of the physics. Here, the same checker verifies the outputs of other solvers on the same problem. Specifically, FEniCSx computes both fields and receives the same bounds as our own solver. Five plausible bugs in a correct solver, one of them about 0.2% from the true impedance, all converge and pass a grid convergence study, yet the certificate rejects or refutes all five. Of three solvers written by LLMs, one is correct and certified to 0.1%, and one never solves the equation but converges. Neural networks that predict the coefficients of a reduced basis emit admissible fields and receive valid per-prediction bounds, at most 0.0021% wide inside their training range and 0.3-25% wide outside it, where 90% conformal intervals cover none of 14 tests. Untuned Fourier neural operators with free nodal outputs receive valid but uninformative bounds. On a uniform grid, interpolation onto the certificate grid limits them, and on the certificate grid, thin cells turn small nodal errors into large energy errors. Energy-norm training narrows the certified interval tenfold, and projecting the nodal-loss outputs onto the reduced basis narrows it by two to four orders of magnitude, still uninformative. The guarantee concerns the stated model and holds for any output, wherever its input lies. It is informative only when the output is accurate in energy on a grid that resolves the problem.

infographic.key_insight: A small independent checker converts admissible potential and exactly charge-conserving current fields into guaranteed error bounds, regardless of which PDE solver produced them.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Certificate-based verification can audit third-party, LLM-written, and neural PDE solvers without relying on code inspection or grid convergence alone.
method: Require solver outputs to include an admissible potential and an exactly charge-conserving current.
Independently check the certificate against a written physics specification to obtain guaranteed error bounds.
Apply the same checker to finite-element solvers, deliberately buggy implementations, LLM-generated solvers, and neural surrogates.
infographic.evidence_signal: The checker rejected or refuted all five bugs despite passing grid-convergence studies; reduced-basis neural predictions achieved bounds at most 0.0021% wide in-range and 0.3–25% wide out-of-range, where 90% conformal intervals covered none of 14 tests.
infographic.watch_item: Guarantees apply only to the stated physics model; informative bounds require energy-accurate outputs on a sufficiently resolving grid, and free-nodal neural predictions yielded valid but uninformative bounds.
infographic.paper_title: Verifying the Outputs of PDE Solvers: From Finite Elements to Neural Surrogates

title: Irreducible shallow tanh neural networks are a manifold
authors: Ivan Bioli, Isabella Carla Gonnella, Carlo Marcati, Federico Pichi
abstract: Neural networks (NNs) have been increasingly used as function approximators, motivating the study of the geometry of their function spaces. We study the set of functions represented by shallow neural networks with hyperbolic tangent activation, fixed input and output dimensions, and $n$ hidden neurons. In particular, we prove that the subset represented by irreducible networks in the sense of Sussmann (Neural Networks, 1992), i.e., networks with no redundant neurons, is a smooth embedded submanifold of the Sobolev spaces $\mathrm{W}^{\ell,p}$ on bounded sets for any $\ell\in\mathbb{N}$ and $p\in[1,+\infty]$. The key step is to show that if a sequence of networks converges in $\mathrm{W}^{\ell,p}$ to an irreducible network with the same number of hidden neurons, then the parameters of the approximating networks remain bounded. Finally, we show that this manifold has exactly $n+1$ connected components when both the input and output are scalar, and is connected otherwise.

infographic.key_insight: Functions represented by irreducible shallow tanh networks with n hidden neurons form a smooth embedded manifold in Sobolev spaces, with exactly n+1 connected components for scalar input and output and one component otherwise.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The result provides a rigorous geometric foundation for analyzing fixed-width shallow tanh function spaces, rather than a demonstrated improvement in training performance.
method: Study fixed-width shallow tanh networks without redundant neurons in Sussmann’s sense.
Prove parameter boundedness when network functions converge in Sobolev norm to an irreducible network of the same width.
Establish smooth embeddedness in W^{ℓ,p} on bounded sets and characterize connected components.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical proofs for any ℓ∈ℕ and p∈[1,∞], with no datasets or empirical evaluations described.
infographic.watch_item: The manifold guarantee applies to irreducible, fixed-width shallow tanh networks; redundant neurons and other architectures fall outside the stated result.
infographic.paper_title: Irreducible shallow tanh neural networks are a manifold

title: Categorical Foundations of AI Agents
authors: Yong Wang
abstract: We follow the idea of separating intelligence from execution and give the categorical foundations of AI agents: the transformers, the agents, and the orchestrations and choreographies of AI agents are categorized, and which also include their coalgebras and algebras.

infographic.key_insight: The paper proposes categorical foundations for AI agents, separating intelligence from execution and encompassing transformers, agents, and their coordination.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This framework could support formal reasoning about agent composition and coordination, though practical engineering benefits are not established in the abstract.
method: Separate intelligence from execution.
Describe transformers, agents, orchestrations, and choreographies categorically.
Include associated algebra and coalgebra structures.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract describes a theoretical framework but reports no datasets, benchmarks, or empirical evaluation.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not specify how the categorical structures map to executable agent systems.
infographic.paper_title: Categorical Foundations of AI Agents

title: Revealing Geometry under Strong Noise: Spectral Embeddings and Clustering via Random Geometric Graphs
authors: Hai-Xiao Wang, Xiucai Ding
abstract: Modern massive datasets often contain useful low-dimensional nonlinear structures that are hidden by noise. Spectral embedding algorithms rely on meaningful local relationships between observations, but noise accumulated across many coordinates can make the observed distances unreliable. This also complicates clustering when groups have curved or concentric shapes and cannot be distinguished by their centers. In this paper, we develop a new method that denoises pairwise distances before using them to construct spectral embeddings and identify communities. Our approach uses cross-fitted projections to estimate distances between the underlying signals, selects a neighborhood radius from the observed sample, and builds a random geometric graph whose spectral coordinates represent the latent geometric structure. By connecting nearby points, such a geometric graph can distinguish different groups even when their centers coincide. A novel recursive procedure is then proposed to extract clusters from the graph using its spectral embeddings when such clusters exist. On the theoretical side, under a manifold model, we provide guarantees for our spectral embedding algorithm, which can be understood through the eigendecomposition of an integral operator associated with the underlying geometry. We show that the algorithm is robust to noise when the total noise energy is comparable to the total signal energy or, under additional conditions, exceeds it. To our knowledge, this is among the first spectral embedding algorithms that can handle such strong noise in datasets with nonlinear structures. In addition, our proposed clustering algorithm can recover the underlying clusters even when their centers coincide. Numerical studies demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed method in mitigating noise and revealing geometric structures for both spectral embedding and clustering.

infographic.key_insight: Denoising pairwise distances before spectral embedding can reveal nonlinear geometry and separate clusters with coincident centers, even under strong noise.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could improve embedding and clustering pipelines for high-dimensional measurements whose raw distances are distorted by accumulated noise.
method: Estimate latent signal distances using cross-fitted projections.
Select a neighborhood radius from the sample and build a random geometric graph.
Compute spectral embeddings and recursively extract clusters.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports manifold-model guarantees and numerical studies showing improved geometry recovery and clustering, but provides no dataset details or quantitative results.
infographic.watch_item: Strong-noise guarantees depend on modeling assumptions, with additional conditions required when total noise energy exceeds total signal energy.
infographic.paper_title: Revealing Geometry under Strong Noise: Spectral Embeddings and Clustering via Random Geometric Graphs

title: Convergence of potential-preserving annealed Sinkhorn algorithm
authors: Dawid Lipinski, Maciej Buze
abstract: The annealed Sinkhorn algorithm is an iterative method for approximating solutions of optimal transport problems, in which the entropic regularisation parameter is progressively decreased. As this parameter decreases, one may preserve either the multiplicative scaling factors or the corresponding dual potentials. We study the potential-preserving iterates under positive, non-increasing regularisation schedules tending to zero. We prove that, if the schedule is non-summable, the iterates admit a subsequence converging to a solution of the corresponding optimal transport problem. The non-summability condition is sharp, as for every summable schedule in this class we construct an example in which the iterates converge to a plan violating the prescribed source marginal. We further establish convergence of the entire sequence if the relative inverse-temperature increments are also square-summable, and show by example that non-summability alone does not guarantee full convergence. Our convergence conditions are satisfied by linear inverse-temperature schedules, under which recent work has shown that the scaling-preserving iterates fail to converge to a solution of the optimal transport problem. We also derive convergence rates for polynomial inverse-temperature schedules up to and including linear growth, extending the marginal KL bound obtained by mirror-descent analysis at fixed temperature. Our best rate for the transport cost gap after rounding improves on that established for scaling-preserving annealing. Simple numerical illustrations accompany these convergence results.

infographic.key_insight: Preserving dual potentials during Sinkhorn annealing enables subsequential convergence to an optimal transport solution under a sharp non-summability condition, with full convergence under an additional schedule condition.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Linear inverse-temperature schedules satisfy the potential-preserving convergence conditions even where scaling-preserving annealing can fail.
method: Decrease entropic regularisation while preserving dual potentials rather than multiplicative scaling factors.
Require positive, non-increasing regularisation tending to zero with a divergent sum for subsequential convergence.
Establish full convergence when relative inverse-temperature increments are also square-summable, plus rates for polynomial inverse-temperature growth up to linear.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports convergence proofs, counterexamples, improved rounded transport-cost gap rates over scaling-preserving annealing, and simple numerical illustrations.
infographic.watch_item: Non-summability alone does not ensure full convergence; summable schedules can converge to plans violating the prescribed source marginal.
infographic.paper_title: Convergence of potential-preserving annealed Sinkhorn algorithm
